notes.meaning: In Jesus' story, the listeners are surprised when the master gives the extra money to the servant who already has ten. They think it seems unfair to give more to the person who already has the most.

Jesus explains an important rule in God's kingdom. Whoever faithfully uses what they receive will be given even more. But anyone who does nothing with their gifts will end up losing what little they started with.

The nobleman in the parable orders his enemies, who refused to accept his rule, to be brought and put to death. This picture pointed to the coming destruction of Jerusalem, as well as God's final judgment on all who reject Christ as King.

differ.view: Some view this execution as pointing to the judgment of unbelievers after Christ returns at the end of the age, rather than the destruction of Jerusalem.
Calvin taught that this warning aimed directly at the rebellious Jews, but it also teaches believers to stay faithful when surrounded by rebellion.

notes.meaning: After finishing the story, Jesus walked out in front of His disciples on the road up to Jerusalem. He knew that arrest and death were waiting for Him, but He led the way with courage and readiness.

Jesus and His followers drew near the small towns of Bethphage and Bethany by the Mount of Olives. This mountain stood just east of Jerusalem and was tied to Old Testament prophecies about the Messiah. From there, Jesus sent two disciples ahead with special instructions.

Jesus told the disciples they would find a young donkey tied near the entrance of the village. No one had ever ridden this colt before. An animal that had never carried a burden was considered clean and fitting for a royal purpose.

Jesus told them what to say if anyone questioned them for untying the animal. They were simply to tell them that the Lord had need of it. As the true King, Jesus had the full right to use the colt for His royal entrance.
The two disciples went into the village and found the young donkey just as Jesus had described. His exact knowledge showed that He guided every detail of the journey.
As the disciples were untying the colt, its owners came out and asked what they were doing. The disciples answered with the words Jesus gave them, and the owners willingly let them take the animal.

The disciples brought the colt to Jesus and draped their outer coats over its back to make a saddle for Him. Riding a humble donkey rather than a fierce war horse showed that He was coming as a king of peace.
As Jesus rode toward the city, the crowds laid their coats down across the path. Spreading their garments on the ground was an ancient custom used to show deep honor to a king.

As Jesus reached the path leading down the Mount of Olives, the large group of disciples began to praise God with loud, joyful voices. They celebrated all the powerful miracles they had watched Jesus perform during His ministry.

The crowd shouted words of welcome from Psalm 118, proclaiming Jesus as the blessed King who comes in the name of the Lord. They praised God for heavenly peace, rejoicing that the Messiah had come to bring people back to God.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: Orthodox teaching observes that the crowds rightly hailed Jesus as king but wrongly looked for an earthly political ruler, and many soon joined the call to crucify Him.

notes.meaning: Some Pharisees in the crowd were troubled by these royal praises and demanded that Jesus quiet His disciples. They refused to accept Him as Messiah and worried that calling Him king would cause dangerous trouble with Rome.

Jesus answered that the praises could not be stopped, saying that the stones would cry out if the people stayed silent. He meant that God's plan to celebrate the Messiah on that day was so certain that nothing could silence it.

differ.view: Wesley explained that if human voices fell silent, God's power would raise up even the most unlikely instruments to declare His praise.
Godbey argued that Jesus' words show His approval of loud and joyful shouts of praise in worship.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentary notes that this proverb shows nothing could hold back God's divine purpose to give glory to His Son on that day.

notes.meaning: When Jesus came in full view of the magnificent city of Jerusalem, He broke down and wept aloud over it. Even though its leaders would soon reject and kill Him, His heart was filled with deep pity and love for the people.

differ.view: Calvin taught that Jesus wept as Mediator out of genuine human grief and compassion, desiring that all might be saved, while Matthew Henry urged believers never to hold truth in a hardened way toward sinners.

notes.meaning: Jesus grieved that the city did not understand what could bring them true peace with God. Because the people had turned away from the Messiah, the opportunity had slipped away and the truth was now hidden from them.

Jesus warned that enemy soldiers would soon surround Jerusalem and trap the inhabitants behind barricades. A siege wall would hem the people in on every side so that no one could escape and no food could enter.

Jesus foretold that the city and its people would be crushed to the earth, leaving not a single stone resting on another. This total ruin was coming because Jerusalem failed to welcome God when He visited them in mercy.

After arriving at the city, Jesus entered the temple grounds and drove out the merchants who were selling animals. Holy courtyards meant for worshipping God had been turned into a noisy and dishonest marketplace.
Jesus reminded the merchants that the Scriptures call God's temple a house of prayer for people to meet with Him. Instead, dishonest business had turned the sacred place into a hideout for thieves.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Ambrose taught that the temple also pictures the human soul, which must be cleared of greed and dishonest gain so God can live within it.

notes.meaning: During the days before Passover, Jesus went into the temple courts every single day to teach the crowds. At the same time, the chief priests and respected leaders were plotting how to have Him killed because He challenged their authority.
The leaders could not find an easy way to arrest Jesus because the common people stayed right beside Him. The crowds were so eager to hear His teachings that they hung on every word He spoke.
